19649-the-captain-of-the-kansas:
Louis Tracy was a British writer of popular adventure and mystery novels. His 1906 novel The Captain of the Kansas is a sea story built around shipboard life and romance. A sampler of its pages shows bright drawing-room talk at sea. One young woman jokes that she makes a most fascinating invalid. Banter like that carries much of the book's charm.

Tracy sold stories on pace, charm, and cliff-edge turns. A liner setting let him mix social comedy with danger at sea. Edwardian readers bought his novels in large numbers. This one shows why: light dialogue on deck, trouble never far off. It is a clean sample of the popular sea romance of its time.
19757-return-loads-to-increase-transport:
Trucks that haul goods one way often return empty. Return Loads addresses that waste in wartime America. The Council of National Defense, through its Highways Transport Committee, built a system against empty running. State councils of defense, chambers of commerce, and war boards cooperated. Their aim was to use highways to strengthen the nation's transport resources.

Rail lines were strained during the First World War. Loaded returns could free rail capacity and save fuel, tires, and labor. The plan linked local groups into one working network. Pamphlets like this show home-front logistics in detail. Moving food and materiel was a weapon of war too. This is the paperwork of that effort, preserved.
20218-history-of-the-incas:
Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa wrote History of the Incas for King Philip II of Spain. His contents list opens with a dedicatory letter to that king. Early chapters divide the history and describe the ancient land. One chapter tells of a lost Atlantic island and its first peoples.

Later chapters give the fable of Peru's first peoples in their own telling. Sarmiento wrote from Quechua accounts gathered in Peru itself. His work is a key early source on Inca kings and myths. Readers get Inca history as a Spanish captain recorded it in the 1570s.
20979-brother-copas:
The master of St. Hospital-by-Merton sharpens his Trinity Gaudy sermon in Brother Copas. Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch gives Eustace Blanchminster a quick, fastidious sense of style. Pains over each phrase mark the cleric's care as the tale opens.

Copas, a lay brother of the hospital, stands at the tale's warm heart. Q sets cloister calm against the claims of love and the world. His prose, rich yet clear, dignifies small lives and old stones. Brother Copas shows Quiller-Couch in his tender vein, a tale of faith, duty, and a heart that outgrows its walls.
21356-nat-the-naturalist-a-boy-s-adventu:
Nat is an orphan raised by an aunt who dislikes boys and an uncle who loves him. He already collects specimens when his aunt's brother, a famous naturalist back from South America, comes home. George Manville Fenn lets the boy help stuff and catalogue the new specimens and beg his way onto the next expedition. Shooting and sailing lessons follow.

They sail by P and O liner from Marseilles to the Java Seas and buy a small boat. There they spend years collecting birds, beetles, and whatever else the islands offer, helped by a local assistant. When a hostile tribe steals their boat and the assistant vanishes, the collectors must build their way home.
21375-the-weathercock-being-the-adventur:
Vane Lee, sixteen, lives with his doctor uncle in a Lincolnshire village and invents things, not always safely. George Manville Fenn gave the book a second title, The Boy Inventor. He shows Vane taking the church clock apart, cleaning it, and rebuilding it without two vital wheels. At midnight the bell strikes without stopping, the village fire signal.

Fire hoses turn out for a fire that never existed. Later, two gipsy boys beat Vane nearly to death, and for long he cannot say who did it. A naturalist like his creator, Vane makes friends among the rector's pupils while the village sorts out his accident and his attackers.
21387-in-the-eastern-seas:
Walter Heathfield and his sister Emily are pulled from a sinking ship at the start of W. H. G. Kingston's In the Eastern Seas. Their father dies, kin in London show no care, and a kind uncle soon dies too. The captain who saved them takes the pair into his own family.

He then carries them on his next voyage, bound for the East Indies on the Bussorah Merchant. A fellow guest, Mr Nicholas Hooker, is a keen student of nature. He points out the plants and beasts they meet on the way. Storms, strange coasts, and sea perils fill this long, warm tale.
21504-my-first-voyage-to-southern-seas:
A London merchant's sudden death opens W. H. G. Kingston's My First Voyage to Southern Seas. The family lived near Blackheath, above Greenwich and the Thames. The eldest son had gone to sea and vanished; some thought him dead.

The second son, our hero, ships as a midshipman in the 1850s, the age of sail. Rumour and chance lead him toward his lost brother, held captive far away. Pirates, drunken captains, and wrecks crowd the long tale, with fine views of Ceylon. Kingston's seamanship, as ever, is exact, and the action never drags.
21784-the-goblins-christmas:
Goblins hold a wild Christmas frolic in this rhymed picture book by Elizabeth Anderson, published at Los Angeles in 1908. A big bright moon hangs over tall pines as the Man in the Moon calls the spooks out for a merry dance. A witch and a goblin lead the sprites down the Milky Way. A black caldron boils high enough to light the sky.

Alexander Sharp's pictures follow the fun: a fairy queen, sprites and toadstools, a boy and a rabbit, an elf and a spider. Anderson wrote the book for two children, Earl and Georgia, who loved fairies in the grass. The verse is spooky without real fright. It is a playful American fairy book from the age of color picture books.
22033-plotting-in-pirate-seas:

The trail leads through the ruined citadel of King Christophe and out to the old buccaneer island of Tortuga. Cuba follows, with plots thickening in pirate seas once ruled by men like Morgan. Texas in 1835 rose against Mexican rule. The Alamo, Goliad, and San Jacinto gave the struggle its immortal names, and Stratemeyer's lads stand near them all.

The publisher's lists at the front advertise Stratemeyer's many series at a dollar and a quarter a volume. Inside, the story mixes real commanders with invented boys on scout and courier duty. Such books taught history as adventure to American schoolboys. This one keeps the Texas myth in its simple, heroic form.

The narrator's sample fix is pure Crockett: he wakes to find himself on a pinhead of an island, no bigger than a freckle on the moon. Sky surrounds him, except where the water is. The story keeps the backwoods voice that made Crockett a folk hero: extravagant, funny, and impossible to kill.

The voyage delivers it at full sail.
23161-sodom-and-gomorrah-texas:
A snap judgment leads to disaster in Sodom and Gomorrah, Texas. An official had given a snap judgement, the tale says, and it led to disaster. The instructions are not clear. Nowhere, the complaint runs, does all that verbiage state how large a being must be before it counts as a person.

Counting people, in this story, is a technical problem with biblical stakes. Two Texas towns named for the cities of the plain invite exactly the comparison the title makes, and officialdom's vague orders give the comparison teeth. The excerpt's complaint, nowhere does it say how big, could head a dozen bureaucratic horror stories. Here it heads a short, dry piece of speculative fiction about measurement, mercy, and forms filled in too fast.
a-phyllis-of-the-sierras:
Bret Harte opens where the great highway of the Sierras nears the summit and the pines thin into rock and waste. Side paths slip off toward clearings, logslides, and a sawmill half hidden in the forest it is eating. In such a clearing lives the mill owner's family, and his daughter, a Phyllis of the mountains.

An English visitor, in California for his health, is taken in by the family and slowly drawn to the girl, whose direct, woodland ways unsettle his city habits. Harte sets the courtship against mill work, mountain weather, and the father's pride. The tale is one of his gentler Sierra romances, with the forest itself given the largest share of the telling.

Kings, wars, and old traditions fill Johnson's vast, careful narrative. He drew on oral lore, court memory, and his own wide travel. The work stands as a founding text of African written history. An African voice claims the past from inside, with pride and proof. No study of the Yoruba world starts anywhere else with real profit today. Johnson's work survives as a near miracle of preservation in its own right.
la-bas:
J.-K. Huysmans published his French novel Là-bas in 1891. This English version, translated by Keene Wallace, appeared privately in 1928. Its first chapter shows writers debating the book's dark subject.

One speaker defends writing about Gilles de Rais, a notorious historical figure. He also defends the raw language of naturalist fiction. Hospital, latrine, and workshop words, he says, fit the matter. The novel became famous for its interest in evil, faith, and the occult. The debate in chapter one sets the book's whole direction. Faith, art, and horror pull the characters in opposed ways.
lesser-hippias:
Plato's Lesser Hippias is a short dialogue on truth and lying. Benjamin Jowett translated this edition and added notes on Plato's works. His appendix warns that genuine and spurious writings are hard to separate.

Aristotle's testimony, Jowett says, is the best external evidence available. In the dialogue, Socrates questions the sophist Hippias. They ask whether a person who errs on purpose is better than one who errs by chance. Achilles and Odysseus serve as their test cases. The talk ends in puzzlement, as Socrates often leaves it. Hippias prides himself on never telling a falsehood. Socrates turns that pride into a thorny puzzle about skill.
love-s-final-victory-ultimate-universal-:
Love's Final Victory argues that all souls will at last be saved. Its author signs himself Horatio, an orthodox minister. The subtitle states his ground: Scripture and reason, fairly read. A fierce line from Carlyle opens the book as a warning against false belief.

The contents survey rival theories of the world to come. Chapters attack the cruelty of older views on hell and election. They ask what becomes of the heathen and of infants. Conditional immortality and eternal punishment both come under fire. The author pleads for charity toward those who disagree. His book is a bold, kind challenge to the doctrine of endless loss.
madame-midas:
Madame Midas is a novel of mystery and gold by Fergus Hume. Its prologue, 'Cast Up by the Sea,' opens on a wild, bleak coast. Headlands jut into foaming water above a half-mile of yellow sand. Black cliffs rise behind, loud with nesting seagulls.

From that shore the tale moves to the Australian gold country. Madame Midas is a widow who has struck gold and grown rich. Greedy men circle her fortune, and crime follows the gold. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. Here he mixes shipwreck, mining, and murder into one plot. It is rousing colonial melodrama, full of twists.
meyer-us4936961-method-for-the-productio:
Stanley A Meyer's United States Patent 4,936,961, granted June 26, 1990, is a method for the production of a fuel gas. It is the last of the eight water fuel cell patents gathered here. By 1990 Meyer had spent a decade patenting each part of his claimed system.

The method splits water with pulsed power, gathers the gas, and readies it for burning. Meyer said the gas could run cars and heat homes at almost no cost. No outside test ever backed that claim. A patent records a described method, not a proven one, and an Ohio court ruled his claims fraudulent in 1996.
mystic-isles-of-the-south-seas:
Frederick O'Brien opens this travel book with a Tahitian greeting, Ia Ora Na. He calls it a simple record of his days and nights. No science or exact knowledge is claimed, he warns. He went to the islands with one thought: to play.

O'Brien writes of Tahiti and Moorea as the merriest world he knew. Songs, dances, reefs, and lagoons fill his pages. He sailed, swam, and feasted with island folk and odd whites. The book comes before his White Shadows in the South Seas. It is a light, fond chronicle of leisure under the equator's bright skies.
nasa-tm-19660015397-observations-on-puls:
G R Cresswell, of the University of Alaska's Geophysical Institute, and T N Davis reported observations of pulsating auroras in November 1965. Most auroras shimmer, but pulsating ones blink on and off across wide patches of sky. The watchers used an image orthicon television camera, a sensitive early video device. Their study covers activity in the phase after an auroral display breaks up.

Pulsating patches are hard to record on ordinary film. A television camera could follow their rhythm in real time. Knowing when pulsations occur, and how they spread, tests ideas about the particles behind them. The report preserves careful watching from Alaska, then the center of American auroral research.
nasa-tm-19680020531-measurements-in-the-:
Robert G. Stone, Joseph Fainberg, and J. K. Alexander of Goddard Space Flight Center report antenna measurements from a sounding rocket in this paper, part one of a study. The rocket flew through the ionosphere measuring antenna reactance, a measure of how the antenna interacts with surrounding plasma. Readings varied in step with the rocket's spin period.

The variations split into parts tied to the full spin period, half the period, or a mix of both. Which part dominated depended on the experiment setup, flight path, and plasma conditions. Explaining the data required modeling both the plasma itself and the disturbance the moving rocket creates. The authors show plasma patterns inferred from the reactance records.
nasa-tm-19720008960-wave-growth-in-a-str:
Wave Growth in a Strongly Turbulent Plasma is a NASA preprint numbered X-641-71-321, whose author names the scan renders poorly. It treats electric waves moving through a plasma already churning with strong turbulence. In such a plasma, the turbulence itself changes how fast a wave can grow or fade.

The authors derive an equation for the average growth or damping rate of an electrostatic wave in a whole ensemble of turbulent plasmas. Strong turbulence bends particle paths while the wave grows, carrying particles into and out of resonance with it. Because of that, the growth rate depends on particle speeds near the wave speed, not only exactly at it. Two orbital effects emerge: the average orbits shift, and particles disperse around them, together broadening the resonance.
nasa-tm-19720010401-bleed-cycle-propella:
Albert F Kascak and Annie J Easley of the Lewis Research Center calculated pump performance for a gas core nuclear rocket in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2517. In that engine concept, the nuclear fuel itself is a hot gas. Propellant must be pumped to extreme pressures to feed it. A bleed cycle taps some propellant to drive the pump turbines. The study covered pressures from five hundred to five thousand atmospheres.

For an engine pressure of one thousand atmospheres, the numbers came out clearly. The bleed flow cost about a tenth of the specific impulse. Pump work and propellant preheat needs were also computed. At very high performance levels, extra energy sat available in the moderator. Gamma rays and neutrons supplied that surplus.
nasa-tm-19720019611-as-511-facilities-an: AS-511 Facilities and Environmental Measurements Program is a NASA document listing the monitoring planned for an Apollo Saturn flight. AS-511 was the vehicle stack for the Apollo 16 mission. The catalog record describes a list of facilities and environmental measurements to watch during the effort. Each entry carries an identification number and a description. It also gives the sensor's working range and the recorder type used. Drawings show where each measurement sits. The hosted sample is unreadable scan noise. No readable list entries survive in the sample provided.
nature-cure-philosophy-practice-based-on: Nature Cure, by Henry Lindlahr, carries the subtitle Philosophy and Practice Based on the Unity of Disease and Cure. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title and subtitle alone state the claim: disease has one root, and cure follows the same unity. No year for the book is given in the sample or the record. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
nibsy-s-christmas:
Jacob August Riis first published Nibsy's Christmas in 1893, and Books for Libraries Press reprinted it at Freeport, New York, in 1969. A picture shows Nibsy dressed as Santa Claus. Riis inscribed the tale to Queen Louise of Denmark, friend of the afflicted in his childhood home.

The story opens on Christmas Eve on New York's East Side. Darkness closes in on a cold, hard day. Light from a delicatessen and a corner saloon falls on men with empty dinner pails. They hurry home with coats buttoned tight, heads bent against the blast from the river. Christmas in the tenements is Riis's ground.
novelas-cortas:
Don Pedro A. de Alarcón, a member of the Spanish Academy, wrote the short novels in Novelas Cortas. W. F. Giese, of the University of Wisconsin, edited this school edition with notes and a vocabulary. Ginn and Company published it in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London. Spanish students were its first readers.

Contents open with La Buenaventura, then La Corneta de Llaves and Las Dos Glorias. El Afrancesado, Viva el Papa, and El Extranjero follow. El Libro Talonario and Moros y Cristianos come next, the latter the longest piece. El Año en Spitzberg closes the tales. An idiomatic commentary at the back explains hard phrases for learners.
old-christmas:
Washington Irving wrote these sketches of an English Christmas. They are set at Bracebridge Hall in the countryside. The contents move from the stage coach to Christmas dinner. Irving laments that old holiday customs are fading fast. He recalls games, feasts, and rural joys of former times.

The sketches show hosts, guests, and poor neighbors at the feast. Good fires, rich food, and welcome for all fill the hall. It says the pieces helped shape the American idea of Christmas. Warmth and gentle humor run through every scene. An old song in the text bids welcome to the poor. It says the poor were not chased from the gates.
omoo-adventures-in-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville wrote this sea narrative about the South Seas. The contents list dozens of chapters aboard the Julia. Early chapters describe the ship, crew, and forecastle life. The ship touches at Dominica and other islands. Tattooers, gales, and coral islands fill the voyage.

Later chapters center on Tahiti and the town of Papeetee. The crew defies the consul and faces the French. Some sailors land in the local calaboose prison. Doctor Long Ghost provides humor among the men. Melville draws on his own whaling years for detail. The book mixes adventure, satire, and island life.
on-the-indian-sect-of-the-jainas:
Georg Bühler wrote this essay on the Jaina sect of India. He read it in Vienna on May 26, 1887. James Burgess edited this English translation in 1903. Burgess also added an outline of Jaina mythology. Bühler knew the Jains and their religious books well.

The preface hopes Indian readers will welcome the translation. German works were sealed books to most of them, Burgess says. The essay gives a succinct account of the sect. Its long note defends the Jaina tradition as authentic. Burgess adds a fuller account of the Tirthankaras. Those figures stand at the center of Jaina worship.
podcast-dannyjones-MxF7TzYzfAs:
Journalist Ben Swann joins Danny Jones to discuss the darkest corner of the Epstein record as Swann presents it. It concerns classified videotapes he says Epstein kept. Their contents, in the episode's phrase, would end society if released. Swann argues the blackmail archive, not the trafficking alone, is the real story and the real leverage.

Jones works through what can actually be shown: the cameras documented in Epstein's properties, the tapes investigators reported, and the gap between that record and Swann's fullest claims. The strongest assertions remain unproven, and the recording keeps them as the guest's. For followers of the case, the episode offers the blackmail theory in its most developed popular form, argued by a broadcaster who has staked his comeback on it.
podcast-joerogan-JIArjzI3gas:
Former Texas governor Rick Perry and ibogaine advocate W. Bryan Hubbard join the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2477. Perry, once U.S. Secretary of Energy, now backs psychedelic treatment for veterans. Hubbard has led the policy fight to fund that research. Their pairing is itself the story.

They tell Rogan why ibogaine, a strong plant psychedelic, drew them in, and what veterans report after treatment. The talk covers the politics of getting a banned drug studied at all. The episode shows an unlikely alliance, a conservative politician and a reform advocate, making the same case to Rogan's huge audience.
podcast-joerogan-q7hWj2iS0As:
Lawrence Wright, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author and New Yorker writer, talks with Joe Rogan in episode 1588. Wright is known for Going Clear, his book on Scientology, and The Looming Tower, on the road to 9/11. Few guests bring his depth of reporting to the show.

Wright explains how he researches closed groups and violent movements without losing fairness. He shares stories from years of interviews with believers, spies, and officials. Rogan asks about faith, delusion, and why smart people join strange causes. The talk is a master class in patient journalism, told in a calm and careful voice.
proserpine-and-midas:
Mary Shelley wrote two short dramas on Greek myths that stayed unpublished in her lifetime and appear here with an introduction by their editor, A. Koszul. Koszul found the texts as early as 1905 and held them back for years, unsure of their worth.

The plays retell the stories of Proserpine, taken by the god of the dead, and of Midas, whose wishes turn to grief. Koszul notes that the dramas frame some of Percy Shelley's finest lyrics, long read apart from their setting. Readers get a rare view of Mary Shelley as a verse dramatist of the Romantic age.
protagoras:
Plato's dialogue on the teaching of virtue appears here in Benjamin Jowett's English version, with a long introduction by the translator. Socrates tells of a visit paid with the young Hippocrates to the house of Callias, where the famous teacher Protagoras was staying.

Protagoras claims he can make men better in private and public life, and Socrates presses him on whether such skill can truly be taught. Hippias, Prodicus, Alcibiades, and Critias join the talk, and Protagoras answers with a myth of Prometheus and Zeus. Readers get a lively contest over education, virtue, and the price of wisdom.
richard-wagner-composer-of-operas:
John F. Runciman wrote this life of Richard Wagner, composer of operas, for G. Bell and Sons of London in 1913. He dedicates the book to Harold Hodge. Its contents follow the composer from early life and boyhood through his juvenile works to Paris.

Chapters named for the operas mark the climb: Rienzi and The Flying Dutchman share one, then Dresden, Tannhäuser, and Lohengrin follow. Exile gets a chapter of its own. Tristan and Isolde and The Mastersingers of Nuremberg come next, then King Ludwig, whose aid changed Wagner's fortunes. The list shown ends with The Nibelung's Ring and The Valkyrie.
sacred-books-east-vol-11-buddhist-suttas:
T. W. Rhys Davids translated the Buddhist Suttas of Sacred Books of the East volume eleven, published in 1881. Rhys Davids was the leading British scholar of Pali in his day. The volume holds the discourses he judged most basic to the Buddha's message.

Chief among them is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the long account of the Buddha's last days, his final teachings, and his death. The Dhamma-Kakka-Ppavattana Sutta follows: the first sermon, which set the wheel of the teaching rolling with the four noble truths. Other suttas treat signs of a great man and the rules of the order. The volume is a core shelf of early Buddhism.
story-of-aeneas:
M. Clarke, author of Story of Troy and Story of Caesar, retold the Story of Aeneas in 1898, with a map of the hero's wanderings across the sea from Troy toward Italy. Two opening chapters present Vergil, called the prince of poets, and the gods and goddesses of the tale.

The story proper follows Vergil's poem: the wooden horse, the flight from Troy, the harpies, and the giant Polyphemus; then the great storm, Carthage, and Dido's love. The Sibyl of Cumae and the golden bough come next. The regions of the dead follow. Then comes Latium and the shield Vulcan makes. The deaths of Pallas and Turnus end the war.
the-belted-seas:
Arthur Colton opened his sea book with verses about the hot belt of the earth, where seas laugh and thunder around still islands. Chapter one is set at Pemberton's, and chapter two names a ship, the Hebe Maitland. A hotel called Helen Mar appears and then ends.

Sadler moves through places named Portate and Saleratus in the headings. Captains, a Green Dragon pagoda, a King Julius, and a ship called Voodoo follow. The loss of a ship named Anaconda is tied to a captain who did not go back to Greenough, though another captain later returns there. Linked sea tales, rather than one straight voyage, shape the contents.
the-black-douglas:
S. R. Crockett published a Scottish novel with Doubleday and McClure in New York in 1899. Crockett is also named for The Raiders and The Stickit Minister. A frontispiece shows a figure sailing over seas to his own land.

Contents open with the Black Douglas riding home, then a fair lady and two riding together. A rose-red pavilion, a witch woman, and the prisoning of Malise the smith follow in the early headings. Romance, riding, and a smith in prison promise a tale of old Scotland in which a famed Douglas lord moves through love and danger rather than court record.
the-buccaneer-farmer-published-in-englan: Harold Bindloss wrote The Buccaneer Farmer, dated 1918. In England it ran under the title Askew's Victory. Part I, At Ashness, starts with The Lease and The Otter Hounds. A Council of Defense, The Peat Cutters, and Railton's Tally come next. Janet Meddles, Osborn's Pride Gets Hurt, and Osborn Interferes close the part. Part II, On the Caribbean, opens with The Old Buccaneer and The Presidio. The Gold Onza and The President's Ball follow, and the list stops there.
the-countess-of-escarbagnas:
Moliere's The Countess of Escarbagnas appears here in English prose translated by Charles Heron Wall, who adds short introductions and notes. A head note says the play was acted before the court at Saint-Germain-en-Laye on December 2, 1671. It played at the Palais Royal on July 8, 1672. It was first printed in 1682, after the author's death. The scene is set at Angouleme.

The cast shows the Countess with two suitors, the tax receiver Mr. Harpin and the councillor Mr. Thibaudier, while the Viscount loves Julia and Julia loves him back. Scene I opens on the pair at a meeting place. Julia scolds her lover, calling him Cleante, for coming last to their meeting. He pleads that an old bore of rank stopped him on the road, hungry to retail absurd court news.
the-cruise-of-the-kawa-wanderings-in-the: Walter E. Traprock's The Cruise of the Kawa, wanderings in the South Seas dated 1921, carries seventeen illustrations and a map, plus a frontispiece showing the author and his bride. A dedication names three girls, with name translations: Kippiputuona, daughter of pearl and coral; Lupoba-Tilaana, mist on the mountain; and Babai-Alova-Babai, essence of Alova. A publisher's note remarks on the spell the South Seas have cast on readers and the house's sole rights to Traprock's manuscript. Only the front matter and that note are present here.
the-death-wake-or-lunacy-a-necromaunt-in: Thomas T. Stoddart wrote The Death-Wake, or Lunacy, a necromaunt in three chimeras, printed in London by John Lane and in Chicago by Way and Williams in 1895, with an introduction by Andrew Lang. A motto from Shakespeare stands at the front. Lang contributes a poem headed Piscatori Piscator, hailing a fellow angler by the Tweed, by Elibank and Yair, whose boyhood found the waters clean and whose age deplored them foul with dye. Only the title page and Lang's poem are present here.
the-headless-horseman-a-strange-tale-of-:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Headless Horseman, subtitled a strange tale of Texas, dated 1865. The prologue opens at midnight on the prairie, where a stag of Texas is startled from sleep by the hoofstroke of a horse. Metal rings against stone, and the stag springs up and looks back at a rider in clear southern moonlight.

Reid holds the sight back step by step. The horse looks perfect, saddled and bridled, with nothing amiss. The rider, though, lacks something that fills the animal with fear and wonder. What is wanting is the head. The prologue sets a tale of dread on the open plains, told through the eyes of a watching animal.
the-life-of-stephen-a-douglas: William Gardner wrote his life of Stephen A. Douglas, the Illinois senator famous for debates with Abraham Lincoln. Only a Project Gutenberg header is present here, giving the book title, Gardner name, and an April 2001 electronic release note. The header also names the volunteer who prepared the text for release. The biography itself, covering Douglas rise, the Kansas Nebraska fight, and his 1860 presidential run, cannot be read in this record at all.
the-ned-m-keown-stories-traits-and-stori:
William Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry fills volume 3 of his collected works, in an edition dated 1881. Its contents name five stories: Ned M'Keown, The Three Tasks, Shane Fadh's Wedding, Larry M'Farland's Wake, and The Battle of the Factions. The volume's introduction, written by Carleton himself, explains why such a book needs a word of preparation.

Carleton undertakes the task, he says, more for his country's sake than his own. English and Scotch readers especially need help understanding how the Irish peasantry think, feel, and live. He rejoices that demand for a new edition lets him attack the absurd prejudices held against his countrymen from time immemorial.
the-orations-of-lysias: The Orations of Lysias appear here in a literal English translation, in a series called Handy Literal Translations. No translator is named in the pages present. A contents list is present, and the speeches themselves are not. The list names the Funeral Oration and speeches For Callias, The Olive Tree, and speeches against Eratosthenes, Agoratus, and Alcibiades, plus The Grain Dealers and The Cripple. Lysias was an Athenian speech writer whose clients faced court cases and public charges.
the-pension-beaurepas:
An 1886 Macmillan edition presents The Pension Beaurepas, a tale of a Geneva boarding house. No author is named in the pages present. The narrator is a poor young man with a fancy for a literary career. He chose the cheap pension because a boarding house is a capital place to study human nature. Stendhal had given his sister the same advice.

The Pension Beaurepas stood in its own little garden near the lake, esteemed and sociable. Guests, though, entered through the kitchen smells. Madame Beaurepas was seventy-three and had kept lodgers for forty years. She was slightly deaf and fond of a surreptitious pinch of snuff. She asked only that guests pay their bills, use the door mat, and fold their napkins. Her house promises a study of characters.
the-princess-pocahontas: Virginia Watson's The Princess Pocahontas, drawn and decorated by George Wharton Edwards, opens with its title page and a contents list. The chapters promise The Return of the Warriors, Pocahontas and the Medicine Man, and Running the Gauntlet. Later entries name John Smith's Temptation, Pocahontas Defies Powhatan, and Pocahontas Visits Jamestown. Only these first leaves are present in the pages at hand; the tale's own first chapter does not appear.
the-spirit-of-christmas: Henry Van Dyke's Christmas book was published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York, copyrighted in 1905 and issued again in 1911. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. They name a dream-story called The Christmas Angel. An essay on Christmas-giving and Christmas-living follows, with a short sermon on keeping Christmas. Two Christmas prayers, for the home and for lonely folk, close the list at the dream-story's heading, so the pieces themselves do not appear.
the-story-of-pocahontas:
Charles Dudley Warner tells Pocahontas's life plainly. The simple story, he argues, is romantic enough. It needs no extras from Captain Smith's vanity. It needs none from descendants proud of a rivulet of her blood. Witnesses of her time agree on her gifts, he says. She was a remarkably clever child. Early on she showed a tender regard for the English. She rendered them service, willing and unwilling.

Warner notes the London portrait. Simon de Passe engraved it in 1616. She was said to be twenty-one then. Warner traces her first mention to Smith's True Relation of 1608. There Powhatan sends his most esteemed child. She is a girl of ten. She brings a deer and bread as a present. The prisoners held by the English are afterwards given into her keeping. The gift honours her father's kindness.
the-witch-of-atlas:
Percy Bysshe Shelley opens The Witch of Atlas with a verse dedication to Mary. She had objected that the poem held no human interest. Shelley answers her in playful stanzas. He asks why a kitten must catch mice before it may leap and play. A young fly, he argues, deserves its brief hour too.

He tells how a winged vision came to Mary's feet. Its plumes faded as the sun went down and the shower fell. Shelley begs her not to grieve that passing beauty. The dedication sets a light, fanciful tone. Readers meet a poem that defends imagination for its own sake.
three-dramas:
Björnstjerne Björnson's Three Dramas collects The Editor, The Bankrupt, and The King. An introduction says these plays grew from years when Björnson's views changed drastically. Two were written during a three-year absence in southern Europe, and one just after it.

Earlier he had managed theatres and campaigned for truer equality between Sweden and Norway. Abroad he read Spencer, Darwin, Mill, Taine, and Max-Müller voraciously. The social philosopher replaced the poet, and prose drama gained a serious thesis. Readers get an account of Björnson reaching that form before Ibsen, with newly opened eyes and ears.
twas-the-night-before-christmas-a-visit-:
Clement C. Moore's A Visit from St. Nicholas appears in a Houghton Mifflin edition with pictures by Jessie Willcox Smith. An introduction tells how a New York company gathered at Moore's tomb one Christmas Eve. Standing together, they recited the poem aloud.

Moore, born near Chelsea Square in 1781, lived in the same great house all his life. He expected fame, if any, from his Hebrew dictionary, not from a children's poem. The introduction notes that he loved writing verse for his own children even more. Readers meet the famous night-before-Christmas verses with the poet's quiet scholarly life set out first.
typee-a-romance-of-the-south-seas:
Herman Melville's Typee, a romance of the South Seas, begins with a preface written after three years spent mostly at sea. Melville says sailors alone now see stirring adventure, and that his shipmates' warm response to his yarn persuaded him to publish. Fire-side readers, he hopes, will find the same interest.

He warns that he treats the islanders' obvious peculiarities without explaining the origin of their customs. Dates, too, will be vague, since he lost count of the days of the week among them. Polynesian words are spelled to carry their sound to a stranger's ear. The preface frames a sailor's captivity tale told plainly, with excuses made in advance.
uncle-silas:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu built this long tale of dread round a will and an heir in 1864. He was the Irish master of the ghost tale, and this is his great work of the sensation kind. The tale is told by Maud Ruthyn, a young heir in her teens, in her own words.

Maud's uncle Silas, a man with a dark past, gains charge of her life and her wealth. In his lone great house, plots close round her, and her friends can do no more than watch. Steeped in dread from first to last, it is the peak of its kind in its age.
weird-tales-from-northern-seas: Jonas Lie's Weird Tales from Northern Seas came from the Danish in R. Nisbet Bain's rendering of 1893, with twelve illustrations by Laurence Housman. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only, so the tales themselves are not shown. Contents promise eleven pieces. The Fisherman and the Draug, and Jack of Sjoholm and the Gan-Finn, lead. A tug of war, The Earth Draws, and the cormorants of Andvaer follow. Finn blood, and a homestead westward in the blue mountains, close the list.
white-shadows-in-the-south-seas: Frederick O'Brien's White Shadows in the South Seas is shown here through a detailed contents list, with no travel narrative present. Laurie printed the book in 1919, with many photographs. The contents open with a farewell to Papeete and a sea trip on the Morning Star. Darwin's theory of a sunken continent enters chapter one. Later chapters promise thirty-seven days at sea, sea birds, and a first sight of Fatu-hiva. A new governor's landing and a dance on a palace lawn follow in the list.
z-marcas:
Honore de Balzac wrote this tale, rendered into English by Clara Bell and others. The narrator opens by studying a striking stranger's face and name. Z. Marcas, he muses, sounds sinister and unfinished. The letter Z seems to carry an adverse fate. Marcas's first name was Zephirin, and he was a Breton. Names may shape destiny, the narrator half believes.

That brooding start frames a life of thwarted ambition. The tale is dedicated to Count William of Wurtemberg, with Balzac's gratitude. Readers get a short, intense character study. Political hope and ruin turn on one gifted man's failure to find his place.
